title: Given a set of distinct numbers, generate all possible subsets, including the empty set and the full set. Explain the iterative doubling technique that builds subsets one element at a time.
shortTitle: Subsets (Generate All Subsets of a Distinct Set)

s1_definition.oneliner: Start with the empty subset and, for each element, duplicate all existing subsets and add the element to each copy.
s1_definition.profdef:
Subsets generation produces all possible combinations of elements from a distinct set.

- **Power set** is the set of all subsets, and for n distinct elements it contains exactly 2^n subsets.
- **Iterative doubling** starts with one empty subset and doubles the collection with each new element.
- **Snapshot size** must be captured before each round so newly added subsets are not processed again.
- **Defensive copy** of each subset prevents later rounds from mutating earlier results.
- **Optimal output** means the algorithm is O(n * 2^n) which is inherently required since that many subsets must be produced.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, a customer like Rajesh can opt into any combination of add-on services: overdraft protection, insurance, and a rewards card. The product team wants every possible service bundle he could choose, from choosing nothing to choosing all three. They start with one empty bundle, and for each new service they copy every bundle so far and add the service to each copy, so the number of bundles doubles each time.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Subsets is the foundational problem of the Subsets pattern: given a set of distinct elements I generate all 2^n subsets, including the empty set and the full set. I use the iterative doubling technique. I start with a collection containing only the empty subset, and for each new element I take a snapshot of the current collection size, then copy every existing subset and add the new element to each copy. Each element therefore doubles the collection, and after processing all elements I have exactly every subset.

The one detail that trips people up is capturing the size before the round begins. If I iterated over the live collection while adding to it, I would process subsets I just created and over-generate, so I snapshot the size first and extend only the pre-existing subsets. I also make each subset a fresh copy so extending subsets in a later round never mutates an earlier result.

At National Bank of India I used this to enumerate every add-on service bundle a customer like Rajesh could choose, from the empty bundle to the full bundle, so the product team could price and present all options. I generated the bundles by doubling as each service was considered, which guaranteed completeness without recursion.

The key limitation is that the output is inherently exponential. For 20 elements there are over a million subsets, and for 30 there are over a billion. The algorithm is optimal in the sense that it spends time proportional to what it must produce, but one should guard against calling it on large inputs. When duplicates are present, sorting and restricting which subsets to extend avoids over-counting.

Remember one sentence: start with the empty subset, snapshot the size, and double the collection by copying and extending with each new element.

---

keyPoints: For n distinct elements there are exactly 2^n subsets, including the empty set and the full set
Iterative doubling starts with the empty subset and doubles the collection with each new element
Snapshot the collection size before each round to avoid processing newly added subsets
Each subset must be a defensive copy so later rounds do not mutate earlier results
The algorithm is O(n * 2^n) which is optimal since that many subsets must be output
For duplicate elements, sort first and only extend subsets added in the previous round
Bit manipulation offers an alternative where each number 0 to 2^n-1 represents a subset
